readerTitle: The café that changed five things and learned nothing
caseNote: 가상 사례 (카페, 가계부 앱) · 개념 출처는 Eric Ries, The Lean Startup (2011)
insight: 실험의 성과는 만든 양이 아니라 배운 양이다. 무엇을 배울지와 어떤 숫자를 볼지를 먼저 정하고, 그다음에 가장 작은 것을 만든다.
misconception: 많이 바꾸고 빨리 만들수록 빨리 배운다. 매출이 오르면 무엇이 효과였는지는 저절로 알게 된다.

sources.text: Ries, E. (2011). The Lean Startup. Crown Business. (Build-Measure-Learn 피드백 루프, 역순으로 계획하기)
카페와 앱 사례의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Build-Measure-Learn 루프와 '계획은 Learn → Measure → Build 역순으로 세운다'는 설명이 The Lean Startup 원문과 일치하는지 게시 전 확인하세요.
카페 매출 12% 증가, 앱 사례 등 모든 수치는 가상입니다. 실제 통계처럼 읽히지 않도록 해당 카드에 illustrative 라벨을 붙였습니다.

cards.title: The café that changed five things and learned nothing
body: In one month, Mara added a brunch menu, opened an hour later, ran social media ads, switched coffee beans and put tables outside.
Sales rose 12%. Now the ads and the longer hours cost her money every week, and she has to decide what to keep. Which change worked? She has no idea.

image.label: Café owner looking at five sticky notes and a rising sales line
image.brief: 카페 카운터 뒤에서 주인이 고개를 갸웃하며 서 있고, 뒤 벽에 포스트잇 다섯 장("Brunch", "Longer hours", "Ads", "New beans", "Outdoor tables")과 위로 오르는 매출 그래프. 포스트잇과 그래프 사이에 물음표. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Sales are up. So are costs. What next?
body: You're Mara. The ads and extra hour cost about as much as a part-time worker. The other changes cost little to keep.
What do you do this month?

options.text: Keep everything. Sales are up, so it's working
options.feedback: You keep the gains, but you may be paying every week for a change that does nothing. You also learn nothing for the next decision.

options.text: Undo everything, then add the changes back one by one
options.feedback: Clean and clear, but slow, and you give up sales that may be real. You don't need to restart to learn.

options.text: Pick the costliest change, write down what you expect, pause it for two weeks and watch one number
options.feedback: You test the change that matters most for your costs and keep the rest running. You'll know whether the money is earning its keep.

cards.title: Busy is not the same as learning.
body: Mara did plenty of building. What she skipped was the rest: she never said what each change should do, and she watched only one number, total sales.
When five things move at once and you track only the total, the result can't tell you anything. Good month or bad, she ends up guessing.
Her loop never closed. She built, but she didn't **measure** anything that could teach her.

cards.title: Build, measure, learn
body: **Build, measure, learn** is a loop. Build a small change. Measure what customers actually do. Learn: decide to keep it, change it or drop it. Then go again.
Eric Ries made the loop famous in his 2011 book *The Lean Startup*. His point: progress is measured in what you learn, not in how much you ship. A fast loop beats fast building.

image.label: A three-step loop: Build, Measure, Learn
image.brief: 원형 순환 도식. "Build" → "Measure" → "Learn" 세 칸이 화살표로 이어지고 다시 Build로 돌아옴. 원 가운데에 "Decide: keep, change, drop". 깔끔한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Run it, but plan it backwards.
body: The loop runs build → measure → learn. Ries suggests planning it in reverse:
list: **Learn:** What question do you need answered?
**Measure:** Which number answers it, and what result would change your mind?
**Build:** What is the smallest change that produces that number?
cards.callout: Write your prediction down before you start. Then the result can surprise you.

cards.title: Mara tries again.
body: Her question: *do the ads bring new customers, or do they just reach people who come anyway?*
Her number: first-time customers per week. Staff ask one question at the till and keep a tally. Her prediction: if the ads work, first-timers drop by at least a third when they're paused.
She pauses the ads for two weeks. First-timers barely move. She cuts the ads and moves that money to the extra hour, which becomes her next test.

cards.title: Loops need a clear signal.
body: Small numbers jump around. A rainy week or a local festival can swamp a two-week test, so look for big differences and repeat when unsure.
Pick a number tied to a decision. Likes, visits and downloads can rise while nothing that matters changes.
And not everything needs a loop. Fixing a broken oven or a safety problem is simply the job. Testing forever is another way to avoid deciding.

cards.title: Now it's a budgeting app.
body: Your team ships a new feature every two weeks. Downloads are rising, but you can't say which features keep users coming back.
What should the next two weeks look like?

options.text: Ship the three most requested features to keep momentum
options.feedback: The team stays busy and users see progress, but you repeat the café's mistake: many changes, no way to tell which one mattered.

options.text: Ask: do savings goals bring users back in week two? Show a simple goal button to half of new users and compare
options.feedback: One question, one number, one small build. You give up some speed on features to get an answer you can act on.

options.text: Survey users on which feature they would use most
options.feedback: Cheap and quick, and it can suggest what to test. But people's guesses about their own behavior often miss. Measure what they do.

cards.title: Count what you learn, not what you build.
body: Decide what you need to know and which number would tell you. Then build the smallest thing that moves that number.
**Try it today:** pick one change you made recently. Write the question it should answer, the number to watch, and the result that would make you undo it.
